This year’s profit share payout marks a 10% rise on the £181 million paid out in April 2025.

Life and pensions firm Royal London is to share out £199 million with around 2.4 million customers after annual earnings jumped by nearly a fifth.
The mutual – the founding partner of the first British & Irish Lions Women’s Team – will make the payouts into its customers’ pensions and stocks and shares ISAs on April 1, bringing the total paid under the profit share scheme to more than £2 billion since 2007.
It comes after Royal London grew operating profit by 18% to £327 million as new business sales rose 13% to £12.2 billion.
Underlying pre-tax profits lifted by £1 million to £261 million.
This year’s profit share payout marks a 10% rise on the £181 million paid out in April 2025.
Barry O’Dwyer, group chief executive, said: “We’re owned by our customers and, when we do well, they share in our success.
“In April, we will share £199 million with eligible customers through ProfitShare, bringing the total shared since 2007 to over £2 billion – a tangible demonstration of mutuality in action.”
The group said its workplace pensions business was its “largest source of new customers”, with 230,000 new policyholders taken on in 2025, taking the total to 2.2 million.
Last September it also launched its new stocks and shares ISA, which also qualifies for profit share payouts.
The group added it was launching its “targeted support” offering this year under a new scheme being introduced by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to act as a bridge between generic guidance and individual advice.
Royal London said: “Following the changes announced in the budgets over the last 18 months – around inheritance tax, cash ISA contributions and salary sacrifice pension contributions – it is likely that many people will need to reassess the ways in which they save for the future.
“However, with only 9% of the UK population paying for personal financial advice, the vast majority of customers are navigating complex financial decisions on their own.
“Our modelling suggests that Targeted Support could benefit 21.5 million people in the UK through the actionable advice it provides.
“In 2026, we will launch our Targeted Support offering, designed to complement our continued commitment to offering advisers the support and tools they need to deliver positive outcomes to their clients.”

Royal London pays £751m in protection claims in 2024
Momodou Musa Touray 23 June 2025
Royal London paid out more than £751m in protection claims last year, according to figures published today (23 June) by the mutual insurer.
The payouts supported 65,385 families and businesses through bereavement, illness and income disruption in 2024, with 98.7% of all claims accepted.
This marks the first claims data to partially reflect policies from Aegon’s individual protection business, which formally transferred to Royal London on 1 July 2024.
In 2024, Royal London paid:
£270m in term life and terminal-illness claims, with average payouts of £93,000 for life claims and £132,000 for terminal illness.
£180m in critical-illness claims, helping 2,675 customers. The average payout was £67,000, with cancer accounting for 64% of claims, followed by heart attack (10%) and stroke (9%). The critical-illness claims payout rate stood at 89.7%.
£8m in income protection claims, supporting 1,259 customers. The payout rate was 86.8%.
£286m in whole-of-life claims, with 99.98% paid. The average payout was £5,000.
Royal London’s Helping Hand service, which provides health and wellbeing support throughout the policy, saw over 5,000 customer registrations in 2024.
The service includes virtual GP appointments, physiotherapy and support for carers. In 2024, Royal London expanded Helping Hand to include proactive services such as mental-health support via Thrive and musculoskeletal guidance from TrackActiveMe.
Claims data also highlighted the importance of protection across age groups. The youngest claimant was 19 years old, and a quarter of all claims were for individuals under 45.
Craig Paterson, chief underwriter at Royal London, said: “Publishing our claims statistics shows how crucial it is to have a financial safety net for when the unexpected happens. Paying a claim is our moment of truth – and in 2024 we delivered on that promise, with a record-breaking year for claims paid to customers.”
Paterson said the firm is focused on improving the customer experience, including faster payments and fewer evidence requirements for life-insurance claims.

Royal London sees sales rise 17% in protection business
Tom Dunstan
Royal London’s protection business saw its new business sales increase by 17 per cent to reach nearly £1bn over 2025, full year results for the mutual has revealed.
The results detailed that protection new business sales increased from the £846mn that was recorded in 2024 to £991mn last year.
This rise was attributed to Royal London’s proposition and its increase in market share.
This growth contributed to Royal London’s group adjusted operating profit increasing to £327mn at the end of 2025.
This represents a rise on the £277mn recorded for 2024.
Royal London group chief executive officer, Barry O’Dwyer, said: “We recorded another strong performance in 2025 with operating profit up 18 per cent, reflecting the positive momentum across our business.”
He detailed that this was supported by Royal London’s first full year in the bulk purchase annuities market, in which it secured a series of “key transactions” as trustees and advisers valued the stability and long-term commitment that a mutual can offer.
Additionally, the results detailed that Royal London’s Governed Range, where most of its pension customers are invested, attracted net inflows of £2.6bn in 2025, a large decrease on the £3.2bn from 2024.
It was also discovered that its assets under management rose from £72bn in 2024 to £83bn in 2025.
“Workplace Pensions are core to our business, providing 2.2mn customers with access to our flagship Governed Range investment portfolios,” O’Dwyer added.
“Our continued success and long-term focus as a mutual on customers are enabling us to invest £100mn over the next three years to enhance our workplace pensions offer, allowing us to support an increasing number of employees with their retirement savings.”
This growth was also present in Royal London’s Irish business as it delivered protection and pensions new business sales of £488mn last year.
This is a 64 per cent increase compared to 2024.

Royal London boss takes home pay packet increase of 53%
Barry O’Dwyer received a pay rise to almost £4 million after the life and pensions mutual posted strong results
The chief executive of Royal London, the life insurance and pensions group, has cemented his position as one of the highest-paid bosses in the mutual sector after receiving a 53 per cent pay rise to £3.92 million last year.
Barry O’Dwyer’s salary rise compares with an average for Royal London’s 5,000 employees of 5 per cent.
The pay increase of more than £1.3 million means O’Dwyer is paid 59 times the median reward of his colleagues, up from 43 times in 2024 and 26 times in 2020, according to the annual report.

Royal London disclosed the pay packet as the customer-owned business reported an 18 per cent rise in operating profit to £327 million and said it was handing £199 million to 2.4 million eligible customers.
The payout is equivalent to a 0.15 per cent increase to the pension pots of eligible members saving in workplace pensions run by Royal London, a boost unchanged from 2024.
Executive pay can be a sensitive subject in mutuals. Nationwide Building Society came under fire last year for proposing a maximum pay packet for its chief executive, Debbie Crosbie, of £7 million. Crosbie was paid £2.49 million last year.
“When the company does well, my variable remuneration goes up,” said O’Dwyer, who joined Royal London from Standard Life Aberdeen in 2019. “It’s a very strong set of results.”
O’Dwyer’s package in 2024 of £2.56 million was comfortably approved by members. Just 3.7 per cent opposed the company’s remuneration report.
Royal London revealed that it was sweetening one of the chief executive’s two bonus schemes further, enabling him to make up to 350 per cent of base pay, up from a previous maximum of 300 per cent.
The change was “to ensure [the company] continues to attract and retain executives of the calibre required to deliver our strategic objectives in a competitive and evolving sector,” Jane Guyett, the board pay committee chair and a former investment banker with Bank of America Merrill Lynch, said. The committee also includes Baroness Davidson of Lundin Links, former leader of the Scottish Conservatives.
O’Dwyer said that the message to the vast majority of clients regarding the market gyrations of the past week was to “think long-term and sit tight”. However, the company had adjusted its investment positions at the margin, taking profits in the commodities sector.
Unusually for a pensions group, Royal London has a 5 per cent allocation to commodities and had been modestly trimming its positions in oil and precious metals, O’Dwyer said.
In the year, Royal London put a stop to the client defections precipitated by the departure of its star global equities team headed by Peter Rutter. Net outflows of £1 billion in 2024 turned to a net inflow of £4.1 billion in 2025.
Founded in a London coffee shop in 1861, Royal London is the largest life and pensions mutual in Britain. It looks after about £199 billion of savings.
Savers ready to buy the crash
Savers have squirrelled away more than £10 billion in Royal London’s popular money market fund to be ready to buy shares if markets plunge. Barry O’Dwer, chief executive, said the fund had experienced £3.1 billion of inflows in the past year. “A lot of people are parking their money in cash and waiting for a correction,” he said. Money market funds, which usually pay a return close to base rate, are more generous than the interest rates paid on cash by investment platforms, but are not 100 per cent guaranteed.

\UK faces retirement crisis as Royal London calls for pension reform
“We are headed to having an increasingly large population of retired people with not enough money,” Royal London’s director of policy has said, warning the necessary changes would be politically difficult.
Article continues after advert
Speaking at the launch of Royal London’s ‘Higher auto-enrolment contributions, pension adequacy and economic outcomes’ report, Jamie Jenkins said while auto-enrolment had been a success, the current level of saving was inadequate.
Despite the fact that “businesses and households face significant cost challenges”, Jenkins argued that action was needed now, even if implementation must be gradual.
“If we are facing an increasing number of under-saved people in retirement who are unable to work, whose tax contribution is minimal, and who rely more heavily on state benefits, this will inevitably place a greater tax burden on the working population.”
The 36-page report by Oxford Economics, which revisits analysis carried out for Royal London in 2024, revealed only 36 per cent of defined contribution households are projected to meet their target replacement rate threshold.
The research modelled different reform scenarios for minimum default pension contributions. These were:
Scenario 1 – auto-enrolment age falls from 22 to 18 and the lower earnings band is removed
Scenario 2 – employer contributions rise to 5 per cent, resulting in a total contribution of 10 per cent
Scenario 3 – employer and employee contributions both rise to 6 per cent (12 per cent in total)
Scenario 4 – employer and employee contributions both rise to 7 per cent (14 per cent in total)
Scenario 5 – contribution rates are raised to ensure target replacement rates are achieved
The results showed that while all scenarios increased GDP and investment in UK productive finance over the longer term, they had an initial negative impact.
Similarly, the modelling showed that household income and government revenue both fell in the short term owing to reduced wages.
Jenkins said it was difficult to introduce policies that deliver long-term benefits but impose short-term costs.
“It is the big political question - how do you make a political decision that transcends party lines and works through successive parliaments and governments in a way that everybody supports and carries suit.”

Royal London reports 18% rise in operating profit
Royal London has reported a strong performance for 2025, with operating profit rising 18% as the mutual insurer saw growth across pensions, protection and bulk purchase annuities.
The firm’s flagship Governed Range investment portfolios attracted net inflows of £2.6bn during the year, taking assets under management to £83bn, up from £72bn in 2024.
The portfolios are used by most of the group’s pensions customers.
Protection new business sales also rose sharply, increasing 17% to £991m, compared with £846m the previous year.
Royal London said this reflected improvements to its proposition and a growing share of a buoyant protection market.
Group chief executive Barry O’Dwyer said the results reflected positive momentum across the business.
“We recorded another strong performance in 2025 with operating profit up 18%, reflecting the positive momentum across our business,” he said.
“This was supported by our first full year in the bulk purchase annuities market, where we secured a series of key transactions as trustees and advisers valued the stability and long-term commitment that a mutual can offer.”
Royal London completed 18 bulk purchase annuity buy-in transactions during the year, generating £1.3bn of premiums in its first full year operating in the market.
Workplace pensions remain central to the group’s strategy, with 2.2 million customers invested in the Governed Range portfolios.
O’Dwyer said the firm plans to invest further in the area, committing £100m over the next three years to enhance its workplace pensions offering.
“Our continued success and long-term focus as a mutual on customers are enabling us to invest £100m over the next three years to enhance our Workplace Pensions offer,” he said.
The insurer also broadened its investment offering with the launch of a new Stocks and Shares Isa aimed at both individual and workplace pensions customers.
As a mutual organisation, Royal London said customers will share directly in the firm’s success through its ProfitShare scheme.
In April, the firm will distribute £199m to eligible customers, taking the total shared since 2007 to more than £2bn.
“We’re owned by our customers and, when we do well, they share in our success,” O’Dwyer said.
Customer satisfaction has also continued to improve, with 44% of customers now rating Royal London nine or 10 out of 10, up 12 percentage points since the measure was introduced in 2020.
The firm also expanded its private assets capabilities through new fund launches and the acquisition of Dalmore Capital, allowing Governed Range customers greater access to investments such as infrastructure and property.
Meanwhile, Royal London’s Irish business reported strong growth, with protection and pensions new business sales rising 64% to £488m.

Royal London swings to £4.1bn inflows after SJP multi-asset win
Mutual returns to positive flows on back of Strategic Managed fund mandate and money market demand, while IHT reforms boosted protection business.
Royal London reversed 2024’s outflows to record a £4.1bn net inflow last year, propelled by winning a £4.6bn St James’s Place (SJP) multi-asset mandate.
The mutual insurer’s latest financial results reveal a sharp turnaround from the £1bn net outflow suffered in 2024, alongside a surge in gross inflows from £31.8bn to £42.5bn.
It noted that taking over SJP’s Strategic Managed fund from Columbia Threadneedle last February was a major driver of the turnaround, highlighting how the UK’s largest advice firm can be a kingmaker for asset managers.
Flows were also boosted by strong demand for money market funds and the acquisition of infrastructure specialist Dalmore Capital, which added £6bn to the mutual’s books.
The company’s total assets under management reached an all-time high of £199bn by the end of December 2025, a significant leap from £173bn the previous year.
Royal London also saw a 17% jump in protection new business sales to £991m in 2025, up from £846m the previous year. This growth was turbocharged by a surge in high-net-worth clients seeking to shield their wealth from inheritance tax (IHT) reforms announced in the 2024 Budget.
The insurer noted particularly strong inflows into its joint life second death term product, which helps advisers mitigate IHT liabilities for their clients by covering two people on the same policy. Royal London said the larger value of protection deals in 2025 boosted margins on the business from 3.2% to 7.7%.
Group adjusted operating profit grew 18% year-on-year to £327m, with its first year of bulk purchase annuity deals also boosting the mutual.
‘In April, we will share £199m with eligible customers through ProfitShare, bringing the total shared since 2007 to over £2bn - a tangible demonstration of mutuality in action,’ Royal London CEO Barry O’Dwyer said.

Budget spooked Royal London savers who pulled £400m from retirement funds
Savers pulled £400million from retirement funds at Royal London last year amid uncertainty over the Budget, the mutual said.
It followed speculation over possible changes to the rules on tax-free lump sum withdrawals.
They ultimately did not take place, but Royal London said many savers were 'not on track for an adequate level of retirement income'.
It added: 'Fiscal uncertainty, particularly in the run-up to the Budget, has also meant that more customers have accessed their pension savings early.'
It follows the disclosure by investment platform AJ Bell that its savers pulled about £600million from their pension pots before the Budget.
Royal London reported an 18 per cent increase in operating profit to £327million.

Royal London hits record £199bn AUM amid private assets push
Profit up 18%
Boosted flows into liquidity funds and a £4.6bn multi-asset mandate with St James’s Place saw Royal London hit net inflows of £4.1bn in 2025, following £1bn of outflows in the previous year.
According to its annual results today (6 March), assets under management (AUM) increased to a record £199bn, £26bn higher than at the end of 2024.
This included £6bn from Dalmore Capital, which Royal London acquired in May 2025 to boost its private asset capabilities alongside the launch of new private asset-focused funds throughout the year.
Royal London launched three asset-backed securities funds and entered the collateralised loan obligation market in 2025.
Operating profit also grew by 18% to £327m, from £277m in 2024, which it attributed to strength in its pensions business, higher protection contributions and a full year of trading from its bulk purchase annuity proposition.
However, inflows into its flagship governed range began to slow down, attracting £2.6bn in 2025 compared to £3.2bn in 2024. The range's AUM increased by £11bn over the year to reach £83bn
Of its actively managed funds, 80% outperformed their three-year benchmark on an equally weighted basis and 51% outperformed on an AUM-weighted basis, although these figures were slightly down from 81% and 60%, respectively, in 2024.
Group CEO Barry O'Dwyer said the results reflected the positive momentum across the business, and revealed that Royal London will share £199m with eligible customers through ProfitShare in April.
He noted the group had broadened its savings offering for its Individual and Workplace Pensions customers with the launch of a new Stocks and Shares ISA – which also qualifies for ProfitShare.
"We continue to focus on helping customers to make informed choices to build lasting financial resilience," O'Dwyer added.

Bumper inflows for Royal London amid fears over AI and Middle East
Investors’ quest for safe havens leads to inflows nearly five times the average
Sunday April 05 2026, 5.25pm,
Royal London’s leading money market fund has enjoyed inflows almost five times higher than the average seen over the past 15 years as investors seek safe havens amid the conflict in the Middle East and fears of an AI bubble.
UK’s largest mutual life, pensions, and investment manager recorded inflows of £3.1 billion into its short-term money market fund last year to take its asset under management (AUM) over £10 billion. Market volatility in the first two months of the year led to a further acceleration in flows that brought the fund’s assets to almost £10.7 billion.
Investors have been rotating into money market funds as they seek security during a time of high market volatility, with the Vix index, a barometer of American equity market volatility, touching 30 last week, a reading associated with significant market distress.

Last year, money market funds were popular amid caution over valuations in the artificial intelligence sector and the possible impact of developments in machine learning technologies on incumbent software providers, data firms and publishing businesses.
More recently, these funds, which invest in safe, short-term financial instruments and cash, have enjoyed renewed interest as investors respond to a sell-off in equity markets sparked by the Iran conflict and volatility in the price of commodities and precious metals.
Barry O’Dwyer, group chief executive of Royal London, said investors moving money into the asset manager’s short-term money market fund last year was a “trend we continued to see in the first three months of the year”. The fund had previously had average inflows of £640 million a year for the past 15 years.
O’Dwyer said: “We’ve seen some investors rotate into money market funds as concern grows about a potential AI-driven market bubble, and the conflict in the Middle East.
“These funds are booming because they offer something rare in today’s environment; competitive returns, daily access to cash and a sense of security when the wider economy feels uncertain. This isn’t about people giving up on investing, it’s about short-term caution.”
Technology funds suffered during a market sell-off in February as a new product release from Anthropic, a major AI developer, prompted investor concerns about a wide range of sectors.
Equity funds were hit with outflows of £927 million, bringing the total withdrawn since June last year to £12.2 billion, according to Calastone, the global funds network. It said specialist technology funds were “notable losers” as they saw net outflows of £162 million, equivalent to a sixth of the total withdrawals.

Royal London transfer delay sees adviser complain about service
An independent financial adviser has complained after an internal pension transfer request made to Royal London has yet to be completed — more than three weeks after submission.
Julian Pruggmayer, principal of Financial Risk Management, told FT Adviser: “Inform any insurance company in the morning, and send an application for an investment of £300,000, and it will be completed before close of business.
“Ask for money or a transfer and weeks later one is still waiting. How do they get away with it?”
Pruggmayer was approached by three clients who wanted to move their Royal London executive pensions to personal pensions on March 20. He submitted the completed applications the next day.
On March 26, Pruggmayer received an automated response saying the transfer was in progress but had no indication of when it would be completed.
Frustrated by the delay, Pruggmayer emailed Royal London on March 31 requesting contact details for the complaints department, which he said could not be reached by phone.
Having received no reply, Pruggmayer found a contact number from a previous correspondence and spoke with a representative in the personal pensions and new business department on April 2.
They were unable to provide a phone number for the complaints department or confirm when the pension transfers would be completed, although they did provide an email address.

Julian Pruggmayer
On Easter Sunday, Pruggmayer received an email from Royal London requesting a declaration from the trustees.
He said there was nowhere to sign on the original application and recalled visiting the trustees, who had asked whether their signature was required.
Pruggmayer said: “The fact that most insurance company websites do not clearly give contact details for their complaints department tends to suggest their attitude to complaints.
“Likewise, why is it they are always so keen to get new business on the books but then allow themselves several days in which to deal with other matters?
“Such a pity the standards required by the FCA in relation to insurance companies do not mirror those required of IFAs.”
In response, a Royal London spokesperson said: “Royal London’s complaint process is clear and easy to find with a dedicated online page that includes the options to fill in a form, to call, or to write to us to raise a complaint.
“We aim to respond to inbound requests as soon as possible and this can be more challenging during busy periods such as at tax year end.

“The adviser received an email response to their request within five working days, and the Royal London team have been working with the adviser to gather all the necessary information to complete the request.”
As of today (April 13) the pension transfer remains incomplete, more than three weeks since the initial request was made.

Royal London receives FCA approval to deliver targeted support
Royal London has received permission from the FCA to begin delivering targeted support.
Royal London has received regulatory permission to deliver targeted support, it said in a statement this afternoon.
The pension provider has recently been developing its Wealth Wizards advice arm that will deliver the service to its clients.
Royal London said in a statement that it was still developing and shaping what its targeted support offering would look like and would ‘share details in due course’.
Part of the FCA’s policy sprint last year, Royal London is among a number of providers who have been lobbying for the service that will constitute guidance rather than advice.
Other providers, including Aviva, Quilter and Standard Life have indicated they will also seek targeted support permissions. Royal London is the first to publicly announce it has got the FCA permissions to offer the service.
‘Our investment in technology and digital capability means we will deliver targeted support in a way that is scalable, responsive and rooted in good customer outcomes,’ Ben Hampton, CEO of Wealth Wizards, said.
‘The regime creates a sliding scale of help, allowing people to access different levels of support depending on their needs, and at moments that really matter.’
Speaking to Citywire’s Advice Show in January, Hampton said that consumers need more help than ever before and that was why he was so keen on targeted support.

M&G’s Royal London lawsuit over high-risk platform bonds settled
​
Summarise
​
The case came after M&G bought the Ascentric platform for £86m in 2020 from Royal London.
The case between M&G and Royal London over high-risk mini bonds on the M&G Wealth Platform has been quietly settled, according to court filings.
M&G filed a lawsuit against Royal London last November alleging it did not fully disclose high-risk investment bonds held on the Ascentric platform, as it was then known, before selling it to the asset manager in 2020 for £86m.
An update showed that the case has been concluded on 16 May. Details of the settlement are not known.
A spokesperson for M&G confirmed the case had been resolved. ‘We have resolved our claim against Royal London. We will not be providing any further comments on the matter.’
A spokesperson for Royal London declined to comment.
In the case M&G argued that when it bought the Ascentric platform from Royal London in 2020, the non-standard assets held on the platform were not disclosed in the deal.
The court document alleged that Royal London did not fully disclose high-risk bonds, called Corporate Finance Bonds (CFP), sitting on the platform which were offered by the now-defunct discretionary fund manager (DFM) Clear Capital Management.
The bonds were illiquid and provided a ‘conflict of interest’ with the advice firms who recommended them, the documents said.
The court documents revealed that Royal London was contacted by the FCA in April 2019 about the DFM and mini-bonds, and all mini-bonds assets were later banned from the Ascentric platform.
In its defence, Royal London denied the insurer’s due diligence on the bonds breached any obligations or sale warranties saying the bonds were ‘listed on an exchange permitted by its internal policies, supported by a market maker, Winterflood Securities, and were allowable within its pensions under [HM Revenue & Customs] rules’.
It also argued that as a platform, it did not have regulatory responsibility for selecting the bonds and that the fault lay with the DFM Clear Capital Management.
The case was brought against Royal London in November last year following a tricky time for the M&G Wealth Platform. Almost a year before, M&G had put its platform up for sale, but no buyer has been forthcoming.
Last September M&G disclosed it had set aside £4.2m to cover complaints made to the Financial Ombudsman Service about the platform, and that the platform’s parent company had seen a £12m write down following big losses.
Following the results M&G’s CEO Andrea Rossi said the wrap would either be sold or wound down, prompting fresh uncertainty about its future.
However, in April of this year M&G Wealth Platform CEO Rich Denning ended uncertainty by confirming there are ‘no plans’ to wind it down.
It is understood that new business is now ‘steadily coming back’, according to one platform source.

Royal London makes tweaks to Principal equity release deal
Royal London has added a drawdown capability and lowered the early repayment charge (ERC) for its Principal equity release deal.
The changes are part of the firm’s plan of “delivering long-term value, reliability, and increased flexibility for advisers and their clients”.
The drawdown facility means clients will have the option to access their property wealth more flexibly and can tailor the withdrawals to suit their needs.
The minimum release is £2,000 and the maximum facility is the lower of the initial loan multiplied by three or the maximum loan to value (LTV) available at point of sale less the initial loan.
The ERC period has been shortened from 10 years to seven years, which will give more flexibility for clients who choose to service the interest on their loan or make larger repayments.
The Principal product is available to homeowners aged 55-89 years and 364 days. It comes with no fee and loan sizes range from £10,000 to £1m in England and £10,000 to £50,000 in Wales and Scotland.
The minimum property value is £125,000 – £150,000 for ex-council properties – with the maximum property value standing at £2m in England and £1m in Wales and Scotland.
Any pipeline cases progressing through application will continue under the previous 10-year ERCs. Upon completion, the cases will be moved to the new seven-year ERCs and communications will be sent to inform all parties.
Alan Ritchie, customer life stage and solutions director at Royal London Equity Release, said: “The evolution of our Principal product reflects Royal London’s commitment to equity release as a core solution to meet customer needs. We know that the market must expand significantly to meet the growing customer demand for robust retirement planning and repayment of traditional mortgages.
“The new capabilities – a drawdown option and a reduced early repayment charge period – provide advisers and their clients with more choice and meaningful flexibility. We will continue to listen to advisers and also use insight from customers to innovate in the market and to stand out for customer outcomes.”

Royal London boosts equity release offering
Royal London has announced enhancements to its principal equity release product.
The updates include the introduction of a drawdown facility and a reduced early repayment charge (ERC) period from ten to seven years.
According to Royal London, with the new drawdown capability clients will have the option to access their property wealth more flexibly, tailoring their withdrawals to suit their evolving needs.
And the reduced ERC period provides further flexibility for clients who choose to service the interest on their loan or make larger repayments.
Any pipeline cases progressing through application will continue under the previous ten-year ERCs. Upon completion, these cases will be switched to the new seven-year ERCs, and a communication will be sent to inform all parties.
Commenting on the changes Royal London Equity Release, customer life stage and solutions director Alan Ritchie said: “We know that the market must expand significantly to meet the growing customer demand for robust retirement planning and repayment of traditional mortgages.
“The new capabilities – a drawdown option and a reduced ERC period – provide advisers and their clients with more choice and meaningful flexibility. We will continue to listen to advisers and also use insight from customers to innovate in the market and to stand out for customer outcomes.”

Royal London posts 14% rise in protection sales
Royal London has reported a 14% increase in new protection sales to £455m for the first half of this year, compared to £399m for the same period in 2024.
In its interim results today, the mutual said it paid 98.5% of protection claims in the six months to the end of June.
Payouts to 33,000 customers and their families totalled £415m for the first half, compared to £355m in the same period last year.
Overall, the life and pension provider’s operating profit before tax rose 15% year on year to £166m for the first half.
Group chief executive Barry O’Dwyer says: “For six years running, Royal London has been the most preferred personal pension provider by financial advisers, testament to the strength and quality of our customer propositions.
“When most of our competitors perform well, they reward their shareholders with higher dividends.
“Royal London is a mutual with no shareholders so when we perform well, our eligible customers benefit through ProfitShare.
“In April, we demonstrated the value of mutuality by sharing £181m with 2.3m customers through our ProfitShare scheme.”

Royal London swaps JP Morgan for Artemis SmartGARP on EM mandate
Provider has switched the mandate for its RLP Emerging Markets Core Plus fund from JP Morgan to Artemis.
Royal London will drop JP Morgan from an emerging markets fund mandate after ‘a period of sustained underperformance’, the pension provider wrote in a letter to clients.
The RLP Emerging Markets Core Plus fund - which is part of Royal London’s Matrix range, and currently around £20m in size - is giving its mandate to the Artemis SmartGARP Global Emerging Markets Equity fund in November.
All the firm’s current holdings in the JPM Emerging Markets fund will be divested and moved to the Artemis fund, while new Matrix clients will also be directed to Artemis.
In a letter to investors sent out this month, Royal London said the JP Morgan fund had ‘experienced a period of sustained underperformance ... therefore we have decided to make a change to the underlying fund’.
‘After extensive analysis into alternative funds, our independently led investment advisory committee, which oversees our investment range, has decided to replace it with the Artemis SmartGARP Emerging Market Equity Fund,’ the letter continued.
Having trailed the MSCI Emerging Markets Index since late 2021, the JP Morgan fund ranks 226nd out of 332 comparable emerging markets equity funds in Citywire’s rankings for performance over the last three years.

Active ETFs allow fund managers to try to beat a market index, such as the FTSE 100, but within a product that is cheaper to run and easier for investors to buy and sell than their older mutual fund equivalents.
By comparison, traditional “passive” ETFs provide the returns of an index — rather than trying to beat it.
According to a recent report by Goldman Sachs’ fund arm, assets under management in Europe’s active ETF industry have grown nearly sevenfold since 2019 to €68.6bn. ‘That fund has a lot more flexibility about where it can invest, and the things that have done really well this year are ones that aren’t so interest rate sensitive but have very high spreads,’ said Binns, in an interview shortly before Christmas.
A key holding in her £3.2bn Investment Grade Short Dated Credit fund are bonds financing Westfield Stratford City, the giant East London shopping centre.
‘We were buying these when they were just trading very cheap for the rating and for the features of the bond,’ said Binns, whose funds publicly available for sale in the UK house more than £7bn of assets.
Shorter duration bonds have tended to perform well in recent years, with elevated yields at the front of the yield curve, while interest rate cuts have not materialised as fast as many expected.
However, testament to Binns’ strong long-term track record, Royal London Asset Management’s head of credit has held continuous monthly Citywire ratings for risk-adjusted outperformance going back to 2016.
‘Stronger language’
Binns, who joined Royal London in 2007, believes her teams takes a different view to most others about the credit market.
‘It’s more looking at borrowers as if you’re lending to them, rather than just trading their bonds,’ she said.
‘We have some big overweights to areas of the market where you have stronger legal language.’
Indeed, Binns’ Investment Grade Short Dated Credit fund has an underweight to corporate bonds and a significant overweight to securitised bonds, as one point of differentiation.
Last year, the fund attacted an estimated £320m inflow, according to Morningstar data. Binns says interest in the fund comes primarily from institutional investors who are ‘more conservative’. Indeed, the fund was set up for clients that did not want any high yield and who wanted the ‘most vanilla fund you could have in corporate bonds’.

Gold and silver fall from record highs in metals market whiplash
Volatile trading session sees precious metals give up early gains
Traders faced whiplash in metals markets on Thursday as gold and silver prices dropped from record highs following a frenzied surge in prices this week.
Copper led a blistering metals rally in morning trading in London that pushed precious metals to new records, before a sharp sell-off in the afternoon session that saw gold, silver and a range of other metals slide.
“Volatility cuts both ways,” said Trevor Greetham, head of multi-asset investing at Royal London Asset Management, which took some profits on its gold holdings in the previous session after the record run.
“Gold can act like a risk asset if people need to liquidate holdings to meet margin calls,” he said, citing the big fall in Microsoft’s shares on Thursday — suggesting that some traders may have been forced to sell their precious metals to cover losses from a sharp sell-off in tech stocks.
Investors have poured into metals this year at an unprecedented pace in search of reliable stores of wealth in the context of growing geopolitical turmoil and concerns about the dollar, historically seen as a haven asset.
While gold has been a clear winner, silver, copper and other metals have also been caught up in the rally.
However, after jumping 10 per cent to above $14,000 per tonne for the first time, the copper price pared gains to about 4 per cent, while the prices of metals, including silver, gold and aluminium, fell.
Gold was down 1.4 per cent at about $5,324.90 per troy ounce, having earlier climbed to almost $5,600.
Analysts expressed confusion and disbelief at the strength of the rally and then as prices turned sharply downwards.
Neil Welsh, head of metals at Britannia Global Markets, said the volumes traded on Thursday had been “huge”, describing some of the moves as “ferocious”.
Gold prices have hit a series of records this year, rising by almost 30 per cent to surpass Wall Street banks’ end-of-year forecasts — which averaged about $4,700 a troy ounce — less than one month into 2026. In spite of the rally’s reversal on Thursday afternoon, gold remained poised for its strongest monthly surge on record.
While copper is primarily known for its industrial uses, its recent surge has been supported by an unprecedented level of investor demand and speculators entering the market, according to analysts.
One indicator that buyer interest in copper is starting to mimic that in gold is inflows into copper exchange traded funds. Money going into such ETFs in the US has “exploded” this year, with $1.2bn in net inflows so far, already more than double the $426mn seen in the whole of 2025, according to Sprott Asset Management.
Analysts say an influx of speculative investors into metals markets is one driver of higher volatility. Some speculators in the copper market appeared to have “moved into profit-taking mode”, said StoneX analyst Natalie Scott-Gray.
Some analysts have warned that recent high prices may not reflect the fundamentals of the markets themselves. Helen Amos, of BMO Capital Markets, said in a note that fresh data suggested “sluggish demand for Chinese crude steel, copper and zinc in November and December”, with high prices not necessarily an indication of growing demand. China is the world’s largest consumer of many commodities, including copper.

Amid potential fund closure
Hargreaves Lansdown (HL) has decided to remove the Royal London UK Smaller Companies fund from its Wealth Shortlist ahead of its potential closure.
Senior investment analyst Hal Cook said that HL's conviction in the fund was based on managers Henry Lowson and Henry Burrell's continued involvement, but the pair "are no longer managing the fund and have left the business".
A Royal London spokesperson told Investment Week: "We can confirm that Henry Lowson and Henry Burrell left the business on 10 February 2026. We would like to thank them for their contribution and wish them well for the future."
Richard Marwood, head of UK equities, has taken over the fund's management for the time being but, as a large part of the fund is currently owned internally, mostly by pension funds, and Royal London has confirmed it will sell these assets over the coming months, the fund is expected to either close or merge into a different fund in the near future.
The £314m fund has posted a cumulative performance of 2%, 3.5% and -10.1% over one-, three- and five-year periods, respectively, compared to the IA UK Smaller Companies sector averages of 9.7%, 11.6% and 2.2% over the same time periods, according to data from FE Analytics.
"Investors will be informed of further details once Royal London have confirmed their future intentions for the fund," Cook added.
Elsewhere, lead investment analyst Kate Marshall confirmed Hargreaves has kept the Colombia Threadneedle (CT) European Select fund on the Shortlist, despite the departure of Ben Moore as lead manager, due to its "long-term performance potential".
Fred Jeanmaire took over as the fund's lead manager in January 2026, with Moore expected to leave CT to join BlackRock's European equities team in March 2026.

Pridham Report: Royal London and Artemis end 2025 firing on all cylinders
​
Summarise
​
Despite muted net UK fund sales, ISS Market Intelligence said more money is moving around within the UK market than ever.
Royal London Asset Management (RLAM) and Artemis were the fund firms which ended 2025 in the strongest fashion, according to the latest Pridham Report on UK fund flows.
The widely-followed report found that more money is moving around within the market than ever, with gross flows hitting record highs in 2025 ‘despite weak overall net sales’.
ISS Market Intelligence, who now produce the quarterly assessment, said wealth management consolidation and the changing nature of fund selection mean there are significant opportunities for fund firms with clear positioning and strong offerings.
Onshore gross sales were up over £10bn, or 5% year-on-year in 2025, even as net sales were down nearly £10bn.
Turning to the fourth quarter of last year, Royal London Asset Management posted net sales of £1.1bn, driven by its short-term fixed income and money market strategies.
RLAM’s Short Duration Credit fund, led by Citywire AAA-rated manager Paola Binns, is the top performer in the Sterling Short Term bonds sector over one, three and five years.
Artemis came in second with just under £800m of net fund sales in Q4. The report stated that strong sales for the Artemis Short-Duration Strategic Bond fund added to the firm’s success with equity strategies. The strongly performing SmartGARP range has had particular success attracting new money, with the boutique launching a SmartGARP Global Emerging Markets ex-China Equity fund last month.
‘The wealth industry is changing fast’
Benjamin Reed-Hurwitz, EMEA & North American research lead at ISS Market Intelligence, said that the findings illustrate a rapidly changing wealth industry.
‘As asset allocation shifts from individual advisors towards model portfolios and multi-asset solutions, portfolios are becoming more global and more passive, while consolidation is concentrating decision-making power,’ he said.
‘That transition is creating a highly competitive environment for fund groups. Not everyone will make the podium, but there are plenty of medals to be won for managers with clear positioning and strong portfolio value.’
Among more passive-focused providers, Vanguard and HSBC Asset Management both won nearly £800m of net inflows in the final quarter.
Another trend showing in the US data was investors rotating out of funds focused on US large caps.
The report also highlighted that Hargreaves Lansdown had ranked in the top 10 for net UK retail sales in every quarter last year, which ‘ highlights the success of its direct-to-client platforms and the potential of this channel’.

Royal London paid out £751m in 2024
Overall, 65,385 families and businesses received a pay out, with Royal London noting that these figures represent the first set of numbers that partially include policies following the formal transfer of Aegon's individual protection business on 1 July, 2024.
Of the total, more than £180m was paid out in critical illness (CI) claims to 2,675 customers and their families, with an average payment of over £67,000. Around £3.3m was paid to 156 families for children's CI claims.
The primary reasons for CI claims were cancer (64%), heart attack (10%) and stroke (9%), with 89.7% of all CI claims paid. For children's CI, this was cancer (35.3%), death of a child (12.2%) and child diabetes mellitus type 1 (12.2%).
As for denied CI claims, the top reasons were that a customer's condition did not meet the definition (6.3%), misrepresentation (3.2%) including incorrect or incomplete information provided during the application process which would have impacted the underwriting decision, and other reasons (0.8%), including underwriting exclusions that had been applied to the plans from the start.
In terms of income protection (IP), more than £8m was paid out in claims to 1,259 customers who were unable to work, including existing claims the provider continued to pay, with 86.8% of IP claims paid.
The top reasons for IP claims last year were musculoskeletal (59%), cancer (10.8%) and neurological (5.7%).
Reasons for denied IP claims included misrepresentation (8.4%), a customer not meeting the definition of incapacity that applies to their plan (2.9%) and other reasons, including underwriting exclusions that had been applied to the plans from the start (1.9%).
Meanwhile, nearly £270m was paid out in term life and terminal illness claims in 2024. These had pay out rates of 93.8% and 88.6%, respectively, with an average pay out of nearly £93,000 for life claims and £132,000 for terminal illness claims.
Over £286m was paid in whole of life claims, representing 99.98% of claims paid, and the average pay out was £5,000.
The top reason for denied terminal illness claims was customers not meeting Royal London's terminal illness definition (6.7%). The provider said that in most cases, this was because while they had been given a terminal diagnosis, their life expectancy was more than 12 months.
This was followed by misrepresentation (3.5%) and other reasons (1.2%) including underwriting exclusions that has been applied to the plans from the start.
Across all claims for Royal London, the youngest claimant was 19 years old, with 25% of claims paid for those under the age of 45.
Elsewhere, Royal London's wellbeing service, Helping Hand, saw over 5,000 customers registered in 2024.
Helping Hand supported around 1,000 customers and their families last year with a cancer diagnosis (19%), mental health wellbeing (17%), musculoskeletal issues (17%) and bereavement support (13%).
Craig Paterson, chief underwriter, Royal London, said: "Publishing our claims statistics shows how crucial it is to have a financial safety net for when the unexpected happens. Paying a claim is our moment of truth and in 2024 we delivered on that promise, with a record-breaking year for claims paid to customers.
"While we have always had a strong track record in paying claims, we're always looking to improve the claims experience for our customers, making it easier for them to claim and pay claims faster. For instance, we're now able to settle more life insurance claims without requiring medical evidence."
